issues.legal_issue: A court may direct the examination of an additional witness only when the witness’s evidence is relevant and examination is essential to the just decision, and the discretion must be exercised judicially for stated reasons.
material_facts: The case was a criminal trial alleging that public officials demanded a bribe from the complainant and accepted part of it during a police trap.

The proposed witness owned the land involved in the related civil dispute, but was not the complainant, was not present when the bribe was allegedly demanded or accepted, and had no identified role in the trap.
The proposed witness had not been examined during the investigation and was not listed as a prosecution witness.
The prosecution had examined its witnesses, who had been cross-examined, and had closed its evidence before the request to call the proposed witness was made.
The accused did not explain how the proposed witness’s evidence would be material or essential to deciding the bribery charge; the prosecution contended that the request would delay the trial.
The reviewing court directed that the proposed witness be called without explaining her materiality or necessity and without examining the trial court’s reasons for refusing the request.
issues.conclusion: The direction to summon the proposed witness as a court witness was set aside because her evidence was not shown to be necessary to decide the bribery charge, and the direction was made without a reasoned judicial assessment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 311 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 gives courts broad discretion to summon or examine a witness at any stage, but requires examination when the evidence appears essential to the just decision of the case. The discretion must be exercised judicially, for reasons, and consistently with the ends of justice; the evidence must be germane to the issues or needed to address a failure to adduce proper evidence or bring relevant material on record. Section 165 of the Evidence Act complements that power. Sawal Das v. State of Bihar, AIR 1974 SC 778, applying the corresponding Section 540 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, supports the approach that a court may properly decline to examine proposed witnesses when the circumstances do not make their evidence necessary.

rule.if: criminal_trial and appeal_from_order_directing_additional_witness and witness_unconnected_to_alleged_offence and no_explanation_of_materiality and reviewing_court_omitted_reasoned_assessment

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding was a criminal trial concerning an alleged offence.
predicates.appeal_from_order_directing_additional_w: A party appealed an order directing a trial court to call an additional person as a court witness.
predicates.witness_unconnected_to_alleged_offence: The proposed witness was not involved in, or present for, the alleged criminal transaction and was not identified as a witness to it.
predicates.no_explanation_of_materiality: The party seeking the witness did not explain how the witness’s evidence would materially assist in deciding the charge.
predicates.reviewing_court_omitted_reasoned_assessm: The reviewing court directed the witness to be called without explaining the evidence’s necessity or assessing the trial court’s reasons for refusing the request.
predicates.additional_witness_direction_set_aside: The direction to call the additional person as a court witness is set aside.

issues.definition: When an appeal in a criminal trial concerns a direction to call an additional witness who is unconnected to the alleged offence, whose materiality was not explained, and whose necessity was not assessed with reasons, the direction is set aside.
